en: The names were established. Prince Bimbisāra was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean him, and two to play with him. He grew rapidly, like a lotus in a pond, through these excellent provisions.
When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing, arithmetic, calculation, and finger-counting, as well as to those various arts and crafts of the Kṣatriya kings,

such as: riding on the neck of an elephant, riding on horseback, charioteering, swordsmanship, archery, retreat, advance, handling the goad, handling the noose, handling the lance, cutting, splitting, and piercing.

2r4 (Pravr-v II): ...in the practice of firm striking, he became proficient in five areas; those five hundred sons of ministers also became proficient in those same five areas. He was introduced by his father to the eighteen guilds (*śreṇī*); he [became] the guild-leader (*śreṇī-bhaṭṭa*). Prince Bimbisāra, mounted on the back of an elephant, was departing for the countryside.
He saw the royal officials of King Aṅga collecting taxes and levies, and he asked:
"Sirs, for whom are you collecting these taxes and levies?
They replied: [2r6] ... they said.
"Your Majesty, they pay tribute," he said. "Sirs, summon those attendants.
When they had been summoned, he said:
"Sirs, that king is also a consecrated Kṣatriya, and we too are kings who are Kṣatriyas."

"...you shall cause [it] to be mastered. They reflected, "This prince does not understand our purpose; let us go into the presence of King Mahāpadma and inform him. Having approached King Mahāpadma and having arrived, they...
2r8 (Pravr-v II): [The officials] were stopped by Prince Bimbisāra while they were collecting taxes and levies. [They asked: "Should we collect them or not? He said:
"Sirs, this prince here does not understand the fundamental nature of things; just as you have been doing, collect the taxes and levies exactly as they are. Thus he spoke.

The prince saw [them] returning from the countryside and said to them: "Gentlemen, I did not forbid you when I told you, 'Do not collect taxes and revenues anymore. Why then do you collect taxes and revenues once again?"
"If you say, 'Stay,' then—" [2r10] ... "This prince is fierce and powerful; it is possible that he will cause harm.
They approached King Aṅga and, having approached, said: "Your Majesty, King Mahāpadma has a son named Bimbisāra..."
2v1 (Pravr-v II): [The Blessed One thought: "If he is neglected, it is possible that in time he will cause great harm. He then spoke this verse:

"As long as a tree is young, it can be cut with fingernails; once it has grown old, it is difficult to cut even with hundreds of axes. [He said: "Send [him] with a limb... 2v2 (Pravr-v II): ... "send him!"
"Prepare fodder and food suitable for the horses; here I come," he said.
Upon hearing the letter, King Mahāpadma was distressed. He summoned Prince Bimbisāra and said, "Son, why have you [caused] the king of Aṅga’s servants to be...? (as above).

He said, "Your Majesty, that king is also a consecrated Kṣatriya, and we too are kings, consecrated Kṣatriyas; why should we pay him taxes and revenues? Let Your Majesty simply grant me a fourfold army."
2v4 (Pravr-v II): King Mahāpadma sent a letter saying, "Do not let go of whatever power, strength, vigor, and prowess you possess.
Having heard this, he became enraged and addressed his ministers:
"Gentlemen, prepare the fourfold army..."

[He] began to destroy the horse corps, the chariot corps, and the infantry corps of the Magadha territory; he was destroying it. The populace residing in the Magadha territory sent messengers to King Mahāpadma, saying: "O Lord, Aṅga... [2v6] ...Having summoned Prince Bimbisāra, he bestowed upon him a fourfold army. Prince Bimbisāra, having assembled those princes, said:
"I shall engage in battle with King Aṅga," they say,
reciting this verse.
That man in whom the glory of the family finds delight must be protected in every way; when he is destroyed, all are destroyed, just as the spokes of a wheel perish upon the destruction of the hub.
"I must be protected by you in every way.
[2v8] While he was staying on the upper terrace of the palace, he saw him as he was departing and addressed his ministers:
"Sirs, whose army is this?
They replied, "Your Majesty, it belongs to Prince Bimbisāra.
He said:
2v9 (Pravr-v II): Some recognize him as Śreṇya Bimbisāra, while others recognize him as Sainika Bimbisāra.
Prince Bimbisāra addressed the princes:
"Sirs, this King of Aṅga possesses exalted power."
"...must be slain. They fell upon his camp while he had cast off his armor, and by them King Aṅga was killed. King Aṅga’s fourfold army fled in the four directions.
[He said: "We too are kings, Kṣatriyas consecrated on the head. Turn back, sirs! I shall provide for your prosperity and support."
They were turned back from there. Now, the one who had been appointed as the protector in Campā heard [the news]:
"Prince Bimbisāra has arrived at Campā in due course;
he has bound the head of the King of Aṅga with a long creeper and displayed it, saying: 'This is the state to which your master has been reduced.'"
"If you are going out, then go out.
Having heard this, he was distressed and reflected: "The territory may be lost again, but my life shall not be."

Having fastened his sword to his neck, he departed from there. Then, after Prince Bimbisāra had seized Campā, he sent a letter to King Mahāpadma [reading as follows]: "I have conquered this land; command me what else remains unattained that I should bring to completion.
King Mahāpadma was pleased, and he sent him a turban, a crown, and a parasol, saying: "My son, you rule the kingdom right here; I shall remain right here."
King Bimbisāra rules in Magadha; it is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people and inhabitants. King Mahāpadma also rules there;
it is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people and inhabitants.
3r6 (Pravr-v II): King Mahāpadma passed away. The ministers sent word to King Bimbisāra:
"Your Majesty, your father has passed away; come and take over the kingdom. He arrived. Then, by the ministers of Aṅga and Magadha, [the succession] was established in Aṅga and Magadha...
3r7 (Pravr-v II): [It was] prosperous, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.

From the Middle Country, a certain young brahmin, seeking mantras and searching for mantras, arrived at the Southern Region. In the Southern Region, there was a certain brahmin who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
3r8 (Pravr-v II): ... having approached him, he said:
"I wish to perform service at the feet of my preceptor.
For what purpose?
I shall study the Vedas."
He said, "Do so.
He began to study the Vedas in his presence. Their custom was as follows:
[sometimes they were] city-observers, sometimes fuel-gatherers; until, on another occasion...
At that time, they became unable to recite [the texts]. Thereupon, all of them set out as fuel-gatherers. As they were setting out as fuel-gatherers, [the Buddha asked:

"Who among you are the Bhāradvājas? Who are the Pañcakas? Who are the Upapañcakas? And from which region do each of you come? Thereupon, some said, "We are from the eastern region"; others said, "We are from the southern region"; others said, "We are from the western region"; and others said, "[We are from the northern region]."
"Indeed, sirs, we have seen and heard of various regions, but not the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*). It is said:
'Intelligence dwells in the East, courtesy in the South, backbiting in the Western region, and harshness in the North.'"
"The Middle Country has not been seen by us; what is it like, young man?
"It is crowded with hundreds of mendicants, free from bandit folk, filled with noble people, and frequented by the wise.
There flows the river Gaṅgā—blessed, meritorious, auspicious, and pure—overflowing both its banks."
[The river] flows with eighteen bends...
they said: "Young man, there are those in the Middle Country who are reckoned as wise."

He said: "Gentlemen, did I not say to you previously: 'The Middle Country, gentlemen, is the foremost of all lands; it is rich in sugarcane, rice, garlands, cattle, and buffalo, and teeming with hundreds of beggars'?
[The young man replied: "You said that, young man. But, young man, in the Middle Country there are such bulls among debaters as your preceptor.
In the Middle Country, gentlemen, there are such bulls among debaters that your preceptor would not even be able to face their faces."

3v5 (Pravr-v II): ... was spoken, whereby all those young brahmin students became eager to go to the Middle Country. Then those young brahmin students, having sought out firewood and taken up bundles of fuel, [went] toward the residence of that brahmin...

"This young man says that in the Middle Country there are such bulls among debaters that even our preceptor cannot bear to look them in the face. "Sons, the earth is a bearer of many jewels; the world is filled with the most beautiful of beauties, O Preceptor!"
"Let us go; thus we shall have seen the country, performed ablutions at sacred fords, and attended upon those bulls among debaters;
we shall defeat the disputants. [And] he, having few attendants, said this to those young brahmins:
"O sons, if it is so, take these antelope skins, bark garments, staffs, water-pots, and sacrificial ladles; let us go to the Middle Country.
They took them, and he [departed] together with them for the Middle Country.
Some smash jars of ashes upon their heads;
some avoid him from afar like crows avoiding an archery range;
some come forward to meet him with parasols, banners, and flags; and some offer to become his disciples.
Traveling by stages through villages, towns, market towns, hamlets, and ports, he eventually arrived [at the capital]. That brahmin reflected:

"All those who are reckoned as wise are indeed in the presence of the king. Why should I, having abandoned the root, think to grasp at the branches, leaves, and foliage? What if I were to [approach] the king..."
"I shall approach his presence.
He [approached] the presence of the king:
"Your Majesty, I have learned a few syllables from my teacher; therefore, I wish to engage in a debate before Your Majesty with various disputants."
Thinking, "I shall do so," the king then addressed his ministers:
"Sirs, does there reside within our realm anyone who is a debater?"
[He was] one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, like fire in his knowledge; by him the treatise named Māṭhara was composed.
The king said, "Let that preceptor be summoned. He was summoned by the ministers, and having greeted the king with cries of victory and long life, he stood before him.
"Let him come and engage in a debate in my presence.
He replied, "I shall satisfy Your Majesty according to my ability.
Thereupon, the assembly for debate was prepared, and the positions of the proponent and the opponent were established.

The king said, "Whose shall be the first plea? [He replied: "Let it be his. The first plea was granted to him; he recited a fine of five hundred [pieces], and Māṭhara, having repeated it, pointed out the fault.
"This is improper for you; this is unbecoming; this is not logical.
He remained silent.
Then the king addressed his ministers:
"Which of these, sirs, appears more distinguished?
They replied, "Your Majesty, it is the preceptor Māṭhara.
Thereupon the king became delighted in mind and thought, "It is a great gain for me, a well-attained fortune for me, that such a person as this exists within my realm."
"He dwells in the village of Nālada, O King.
Go; he himself shall be your prize for debate."

He was given that wealth of a debater; people desire prosperity and are averse to misfortune. He was sought after by many brahmins for the sake of a daughter. Then he enjoyed himself with her. While he was sporting, taking his pleasure, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him with very long nostrils.
When he had been born, a birth festival was performed for him in detail, and the name Koṣṭhila was established for him. The boy Koṣṭhila was nourished and raised;
with excellent provisions, he grew quickly like a lotus in a pond.

When he had grown up, he was introduced to writing, arithmetic, finger-calculation, reckoning, the Brahminical sciences, proper deportment, conduct, ritual purity, and customary behavior; [furthermore], in the handling of ashes, the handling of the water-pot, in sacrificing, studying, teaching, giving, and receiving—he became a Brahmin devoted to the six duties. Later, while he was playing, enjoying himself, and amusing himself, a daughter was born to him. Regarding her—
"Her eyes are just like those of a śārikā bird.
Having been reunited with her kinsmen,
she was raised until she had become a grown woman.
She was taught the letters of the alphabet, and at another time, when she engaged in debate with her brother, he was defeated by her.
Then her father said to him, "Son, how is it that you, being a man, have been defeated by a girl?
[At that time] a young brahmin, seeking spells and searching for spells, arrived in the southern region. In the southern region...
A brahmin named Tiṣya, who was proficient in Lokāyata, approached him; having approached and paid his respects, he said:
"I desire [to study];
please do so."

He began to study the Lokāyata system in his presence. It was the custom of those young brahmins that when they were not studying, they would sometimes go to perform ablutions at sacred fords, sometimes go to look around the city, and sometimes set out as gatherers of firewood. While they had set out as gatherers of firewood, this kind of conversation arose among them as they proceeded.

"O Kautsas, Vātsas, Śāṇḍilyas, Bhāradvājas, Pañcakas, and Upapañcakas—whom do you belong to, and from what region? "We are from the South," some said; others said, "We are from the West"; others said, "We are from the North. That young man said, "I am from the Middle Country."
They said:
"Sirs, we have seen and heard of all regions;
slander is found in the western region, and harsh speech in the northern path."

"The Middle Country has not been seen by us; what is the Middle Country like, young man? "The Middle Country, sirs, is the foremost of all lands; it is rich in sugarcane, rice, garlands, cattle, and buffalo. It is frequented by learned men, and there flows the river Gaṅgā—blessed, meritorious, auspicious, and esteemed for its purity and sanctity."
It flows along, overflowing both banks, where the hermitage of the sages named Aṣṭādaśavakra is located, and there the sages practice austerities. [They are] reckoned as wise men.

He said, "Sirs, did I not say to you before: 'The Middle Country, sirs, is the foremost of lands; it is rich in sugarcane, rice, garlands, cattle, and buffalo; it is teeming with hundreds of mendicants, devoid of bandit folk, crowded with noble people, and frequented by learned men. [4v9] (Pravr-v II): ...the preceptor.

"In the Middle Country, there are such bulls among debaters that even your preceptor would not be able to look them in the face. That young man spoke so highly of the Middle Country that all those youths became eager to go there.
They then approached the residence of that brahmin, and having arrived, [they stood before him].

Having set down their loads of firewood in a secluded spot, they approached that brahmin and said to him: "Venerable teacher, you should know that because of this young man of ours, we have become eager to go to the Middle Country. Dear sons, one does not travel as far as one hears; rather, lands that are delightful to hear about should be visited."
"But you must not go.
Preceptor, this young man says that in the Middle Country there are such bulls among debaters that [he claims] the Preceptor alone is the only debater on earth and that there is no other whatsoever."
"The earth is a repository of many jewels; the world is full of the most beautiful things. Preceptor, let us go! In that way, we shall have seen the various lands.
We shall bathe at the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and [encounter] those bulls among debaters (*vādivṛṣabha*).
We shall proclaim [our fame] and acquire gain. Thus spoke the brahmin, who was devoted to his disciples.
Having few possessions, he said this to those young men: "Sons, if it is so, take these deerskins, bark garments, staffs, water-pots, and sacrificial ladles.
Having set out, he would seize certain disputants and yoke them to his chariot of debate.
Some [birds] break the jars of ashes on their heads; others avoid from afar the archery hall like crows;
some [flee] with umbrellas, banners, and flags.
Wandering through villages, cities, market towns, hamlets, and ports, that brahmin eventually reached Rājagṛha. There he reflected:
"Indeed, as many as are reckoned among the wise, they are all in the presence of the king. Therefore, what if I were to approach the king? Thinking thus, he approached the king.
Having congratulated the king on his victory and long life, he stood before him and said, "O King, I have learned a few syllables from my teacher;
[I wish to engage] in a debate.
Thereupon, the king addressed his ministers.
"Sirs, does there reside within our realm anyone who is a debater?
The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, in the village of Nālada there is a brahmin named Māṭhara,
by whom a treatise has been composed."

The king said, "Let that preceptor be summoned. He was summoned by the ministers, and having greeted the king with wishes for victory and long life, he stood before him. Then the king said to him, "Preceptor, are you able [to compete] with this brahmin?"
"By my power, O King, I shall satisfy Your Majesty.
Thereupon, the circle of debaters was prepared, and the positions of the proponent and the opponent were established.
The king said:
"Whose side shall take the preliminary position?
The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, this Māṭhara Brāhmaṇa is old... [the king said:

'This Brāhmaṇa is also well-versed in the nine branches of learning and possesses a sharp intellect; it is not possible for me to engage in debate with him. I shall employ the *vādapicchilikā* (the artifice of debate) against him.'"

He recited the *daṇḍaka* consisting of five hundred [verses], and that brahmin, having recited it back, pointed out a fault. This is indeed a censured point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), namely, the loss of one's presence of mind (*niṣpratibhānatā*) in the midst of debate.
Then the king addressed his ministers:
"Sirs, who among you appears more distinguished here?
They replied, "The brahmin Tiṣya.
The king said, "Let the rewards for the debater be given to him."

"5v2 (Pravr-v II): ... we shall give you the spoils of debate before long; our territories of Aṅga and Magadha will become the spoils of debate for you. However, let this very village of Nālada be his spoil of debate. Let it be given to this brahmin from Māṭhara; from him, let another who is more excellent [be sought]."

5v3 (Pravr-v II): ... thus [it was said]. Having snatched it from Māṭhara, they gave it to Tiṣya. Then the brahmin Māṭhara addressed his wife: "My dear, let us simplify the household affairs; we shall go elsewhere. For what purpose?"
"We have rendered great service to this king, yet we have not been protected by him.
They said:
"Preceptor, for whose sake is this household clutter being cleared away?
He replied, "Sirs, we have rendered great service to this king, yet we have not been protected by him; therefore, we are going elsewhere."
5v5 (Pravr-v II): ... he recites this verse:

"It is better for a man to dwell in a foreign land than to live in his own country under contempt; that place where men do not suffer defeat is indeed one's own country, and there one's own kin likewise reside.
When the Brahmin Tiṣya heard this, he approached him [the Buddha].
[The Buddha said: "Stay! This very wealth of debate shall be yours. But he did not stay.
Then Tiṣya said, "Preceptor, stay right here; let half of this small town belong to you and half to me.
He replied, "So be it," and he addressed his wife.

5v7 (Pravr-v II): "...they were protected by him; rather, it was the brahmin Tiṣya himself who did us a great service by giving us half of his wealth and enjoyments. Therefore, let us give this śārikā bird to him for the sake of a wife.
She said, "Why is she being given to him? These two—"
“...should deprive him of life. We have been deprived of our wealth by him; he must not be given anything at all.
They both said, “You are a fool; what would he know?”
Having treated his words as if they were not words, they gave [their daughter] to him;
he married her with a great display of splendor.
[The teacher thought: "All that was based on his having heard little; however, does this young Tiṣya know the Lokāyata?"
"Venerable sirs, where is the Lokāyata known? [It is] in the Deccan.
He gradually reached the Deccan; having gone there, he asked: "Who...
Having approached them, he said: "I wish to perform service at your feet."
"For what purpose? [He replied:
"I shall learn the Lokāyata.
They said, "We do not teach the Lokāyata to a householder. He said, "If that is so..."
"...thinking, 'I shall cut [them],' as long as I have mastered the Lokāyata system.
Because his nails were very long, the wandering mendicant became known by the name "Dīrghanakha" (Long-Nail), the wandering mendicant Dīrghanakha.
Śārikā, too, [was taught] by the Brahmin Tiṣya.
...he enjoys [pleasures].
