"You are exhausted from the road; eat now, for there will be trouble here later.

Having eaten, he departed to a secluded spot and remained there until their time for the meal arrived, the gong was struck, and they took up their respective bowls and followed according to the order of the procession.

As soon as they had sat down, the monastery vanished; that food and drink appeared as molten iron. Then, while crying out with piteous voices, they drenched one another with the molten iron until the time for eating had passed.
And when the time for eating had passed, that monastery reappeared exactly as it was before, and those monks likewise reappeared.
Remaining there with their deportment so perfectly tranquil,
the Venerable Saṅgharakṣita approached them and asked:
"Who are you, venerable ones, and by what karma have you been reborn here?"
They said, "Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful and will not believe you.
He replied, "I have seen it with my own eyes; how could I not believe it?
They said, "Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, we were disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One, Kāśyapa."

When a supply of affectionate food had been obtained for the Saṃgha and visiting monks arrived, we— possessed by stinginess— conceived such a thought and uttered these words: "We will not eat as long as the visiting monks have not departed."
And so it was done;
for seven days there appeared an unseasonable storm, by which that food and drink became soaked and unfit.
Having squandered what was given in faith, we have been reborn here in this individual hell; such is the possibility.
"Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, since we shall fall from here and be reborn in hell, it would be well if you were to go to Jambudvīpa and explain this matter in detail to our fellow celibates:
'O Venerable Ones, do not let the gifts given out of faith go to waste!'"
"Do not become partakers of such a mass of suffering,
as for instance the Śramaṇas of the Kāśyapīya school. Having promised "So be it" and having made his vow, he set out.

He saw a third monastery, adorned with elevated couches, seats, railings, lattice windows, and round windows, surrounded by various trees, beautified by lotus ponds and pools, resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos,
blazing with splendor like a celestial palace, and he saw monks there, well-robed and well-clad, standing with peaceful deportment.
He approached them with great respect; then they, filled with urgency, addressed him: "Welcome, welcome, Venerable Saṅgharakṣita! From where have you come now?
He related everything exactly as it had happened.
Then, having been allowed to rest by them and his fatigue from the journey dispelled, he was led into the monastery.
There he saw that a beautiful arrangement of seats had been made and excellent food had been brought forth.
He was addressed by them: "Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, are you thirsty or hungry?"
He said, "Venerable ones, I am thirsty and I am hungry.
They replied, "Reverend Saṅgharakṣita, please eat.
He said, "I shall eat right here in the midst of the Saṅgha."
They said, "Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, you are exhausted from the road; eat now, for there will be a danger here.
Having eaten, he went aside and remained there.

When it was time for their meal, the gong was struck, and that monastery of theirs burst into flames—blazing, fiercely burning, becoming a single mass of fire—and began to smolder. Those monks also...

In that very monastery, they cried out with piteous voices until the time for the meal had passed; once the time for the meal had passed, that monastery reappeared exactly as it was before, and those monks remained there in their same peaceful deportment.
Then the Venerable Saṅgharakṣita approached them and asked, "Who are you, venerable ones, and by what karma have you been reborn here?
They replied, "Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, the people of Jambudvīpa are deceitful; they will not believe us."
He said, "I am an eyewitness; how could I not believe it?

They replied, "Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, we were formerly disciples of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa who were immoral and of evil character. We were expelled from the monasteries by those monks who possessed virtuous conduct."

We had taken up residence in an empty monastery when a virtuous monk arrived there while wandering about. Then the thought occurred to us: "Let this one man stay; he will clear our debt for the offerings.
He remained right there until, as a consequence of his presence, many more virtuous monks arrived, and by them we were expelled from that place as well.
Then, filled with resentment, we gathered dry wood, grass, and cow dung and set fire to the entire monastery.

There, many monks—both those still in training and those beyond training—were burned. As the ripening of that karma, we were reborn in the Pratyekanaraka hell; it is possible that when we pass away from here, [we shall be reborn elsewhere].
"Rebirth will take place in hell.
Therefore, it would be well, Venerable Saṃgharakṣita, if you were to go to Jambudvīpa and explain this matter in detail to your fellow celibates:
'O long-lived ones, do not give rise to malicious thoughts toward your fellow celibates; lest you become partakers of such a mass of suffering, just as these ascetics have.'"
Regarding the Kāśyapīyas:
having promised "so be it," he set out.
Eventually, he saw sentient beings in the form of pillars, in the form of walls, in the form of flowers, in the form of fruits, and in the form of ropes and brooms.

[They saw] a [woman] shaped like a mortar, shaped like a bedstead, or shaped like a cooking pot, severed in the middle and being held together by a thread as she walked. The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita also proceeded gradually through the countryside until he reached a certain hermitage where about five hundred sages were residing; there, the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita was [seen] by them.

Having seen him from afar, they began to converse among themselves: "Listen, sirs! These Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are talkative; no one should give him a word in reply. Having made this agreement, they remained there.
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita, approaching them with a peaceful deportment, began to ask for lodging; yet no one gave him an answer.

There, however, was a single seer who possessed pure qualities, and he said: "Why is lodging not given to you? You have a fault: you are talkative. Nevertheless, I will give it to you on one condition: that you do not speak anything at all."
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita said, "O seer, let it be so; I shall not speak further. Then, one seer who had gone on a journey through the countryside gave his small hut to the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita.
"Prepare a bed here.
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita sprinkled that small hut, swept it, and applied a smooth coating of cow dung.
He was seen by them, and they said:

"Gentlemen, these Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are practitioners of pure conduct. Then the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita, having washed his feet outside the hut, entered the hut and sat down, crossing his legs, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Now, a deity dwelling in that hermitage approached the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita during the first watch of the night; having approached, she said: "Noble one, [teach] the Dharma..."
"Teach me," she said.
He replied, "Sister, you are fortunate; I have obtained this lodging through a formal agreement. Why do you wish for me to be expelled?
She reflected:
"This renunciant is exhausted; let him sleep during the middle watch.
Having approached him during the middle watch, she said, "Noble one, please teach the Dharma."
He said, "Sister, you cannot remain silent;
you certainly intend to have me driven out.
She reflected, "Even now this renunciant is still overcome by sleep; I shall approach him during the final watch of the night."
Approaching him during the final watch of the night, she said, "Noble sir, why do you sleep? The night has dawned; arise and teach the Dharma!
He replied, "Sister, I have been completely driven out by you."
She said, "Noble sir, what will happen? If they expel you when the night has turned to dawn, you will have to go.
But was it not said by the Blessed One that one must endure fear and terror?
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita reflected:
"It is well said by this sister: 'If they expel me, I shall go.
However, these are brahmins; therefore, verses connected with brahmins should be recited. Thinking thus, he began to study the section on brahmins.

Neither nakedness, nor matted hair, nor mud, nor fasting, nor sleeping on the bare ground, nor dust and dirt, nor the practice of sitting in a crouching posture, purifies a mortal who has not transcended doubt.

He who, though adorned, practices the Dharma—tamed, tranquil, self-controlled, and living the holy life; who has laid aside the rod toward all beings—he is a Brāhmaṇa, he is a Śramaṇa, he is a Bhikṣu.
Hearing this, they reflected:
"He is reciting verses connected with the brahmins. Thus, one approached him, then a second, then a third, until finally they all had gathered around him.
And they were so empowered by that deity that they could not see one another.
Thereafter, the venerable Saṃgharakṣita presented the Nagaropama Sūtra.
"Monks, formerly, before I had awakened to full enlightenment, while I was alone, in seclusion, and withdrawn in meditation, this reflection arose in my mind:
'Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; that is to say, it is born, it grows old, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn.'"
And yet, these beings do not understand, as it truly is, the escape beyond aging and death.

This thought occurred to me: "When what exists do aging and death come to be? And with what as condition do aging and death arise? As I reflected thoroughly, there arose for me this realization of things as they truly are:
"When birth exists, aging and death come to be; and with birth as condition, aging and death arise."

This occurred to me: "When what exists does birth come to be? And with what as its condition does birth arise? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there came to me this realization of things as they truly are:
"When existence exists, birth comes to be; and with existence as its condition, birth arises."
This thought occurred to me: "When what exists does becoming exist? And with what as its condition does becoming arise?
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of reality as it is:
"When grasping exists, becoming exists; and with grasping as its condition, becoming arises."
Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does grasping come to be? And with what as its condition does grasping arise?
As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When craving exists, grasping comes to be."
"And furthermore, grasping has craving as its condition.
Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does craving come to be? And what is the condition for craving?
As I applied my mind thoroughly in this way, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are.

"When there is feeling, craving comes to be; moreover, with feeling as condition, craving arises. Then this occurred to me: "When what exists does feeling come to be? With what as condition does feeling arise? As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose for me a realization of things as they truly are.

"When there is contact, feeling comes to be; moreover, feeling has contact as its condition. Then this occurred to me: "What being present does contact come to be? And what is the condition for contact? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are.
"When the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be; moreover, contact has the six sense bases as its condition.
Then this occurred to me: "What being present do the six sense bases come to be?
And what is the condition for the six sense bases?"
As I applied my mind to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me a realization of things as they truly are:
when name-and-form exists, the six sense bases come to be;
furthermore, with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.
The thought occurred to me: "When what exists does name-and-form come to be? And with what as its condition does name-and-form arise?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there came to me this realization of things as they truly are:
"When consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; and with consciousness as its condition, name-and-form arises."

Then this thought occurred to me: "When what exists does consciousness come to be? And with what as its condition does consciousness arise? My mind turned back from consciousness; it did not proceed any further beyond that.

That is to say: conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging;
conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; and conditioned by birth arise aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

Then this occurred to me: "In what being absent do aging and death not come to be? And from the cessation of what does the cessation of aging and death occur? As I reflected thoroughly upon this, there arose for me a realization of reality as it truly is.
When birth does not exist, aging and death do not occur; and from the cessation of birth, there is furthermore the cessation of aging and death.
The thought occurred to me: "In the absence of what does birth not come to be?
And through the cessation of what, moreover, does the cessation of birth occur?
As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there arose for me a realization of things as they truly are.
"When existence does not exist, birth does not exist; and from the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth.
Then this occurred to me: "When what does not exist does existence not exist? From the cessation of what is there the cessation of existence?
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose for me this realization of things as they truly are.
When clinging does not exist, becoming does not come to be; and from the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming.

This thought occurred to me: "In what being absent does grasping not come to be? And from the cessation of what does the cessation of grasping occur? As I attended to this thoroughly and correctly, there arose for me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When craving is absent, grasping does not come to be; and from the cessation of craving, grasping ceases."

Then this occurred to me: "In the absence of what does craving not come to be? And from the cessation of what, moreover, does the cessation of craving occur? As I was reflecting thoroughly in this way, there arose for me a realization of things as they truly are: "In the absence of feeling, craving does not come to be; and from the cessation of feeling, moreover, comes the cessation of craving."
Then this occurred to me: "What being absent does feeling not come to be?
And from the cessation of what does the cessation of feeling occur?
As I reflected thoroughly in this way, there came to me a realization of things as they truly are.

"When there is no contact, feeling does not come to be; and from the cessation of contact, moreover, feeling ceases. Then this occurred to me: "What being absent does contact not come to be? From the cessation of what, moreover, does the cessation of contact occur? As I was reflecting thoroughly in this way, there arose for me a realization of reality as it truly is.
"When the six sense bases do not exist, contact does not come to be;
furthermore, from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact.
Then this occurred to me: "In the absence of what do the six sense bases not come to be? And from the cessation of what does the cessation of the six sense bases occur?"
As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
when name-and-form does not exist, the six sense bases do not come to be;
and furthermore, from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases.

The thought occurred to me: "In the absence of what does name-and-form not come to be? And through the cessation of what does the cessation of name-and-form occur? As I applied my mind thoroughly and correctly, there arose in me this realization of things as they truly are:
"In the absence of consciousness, name-and-form does not come to be."
"And furthermore, from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.
Then this occurred to me: "In the absence of what does consciousness not come to be? And from the cessation of what does the cessation of consciousness follow?"
As I applied my mind thoroughly in this way, there arose for me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When volitional formations do not exist, consciousness does not come to be;
and from the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases."

This occurred to me: "What being absent do volitional formations not come to be? And from the cessation of what, moreover, does the cessation of volitional formations occur? As I applied my mind thoroughly to this, there arose for me a realization of things as they truly are:
"When ignorance is absent, volitional formations do not come to be; and from the cessation of ignorance, moreover, comes the cessation of volitional formations."

That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact;
from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging.
With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Then this occurred to me: "I have discovered that ancient path, that ancient [way]."
The ancient path, the ancient track, traversed and followed by former seers;
just as a man wandering in a forested valley might discover an ancient road,
an ancient track, an ancient path, traversed and followed by men of old— he would find it, he would follow it.

Having reached it, he might see an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, well-endowed with parks, well-endowed with groves, well-endowed with lotus ponds—auspicious, lush, and delightful; and having seen it, he would think to himself:
"What if I were to go to the king and inform him?"
He went to the king and reported:
"Sire, please know this: while wandering here in the forest on a slope, I saw an ancient path, an ancient track, an ancient road, traversed and followed by men of old;
I followed it, and as I followed it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient [site]."
"Let the Lord have that city measured out—a royal capital endowed with gardens, endowed with groves, endowed with lotus ponds, auspicious, forested, and delightful; let the King complete that city.
And at a later time, may that royal capital become prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants."
"In the same way, monks, I have discovered the ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, trodden and followed by the seers of old.

What, monks, is that ancient path, that ancient track, that ancient trail, trodden and followed by the seers of old? It is the Noble Eightfold Path; namely: right view, right intention, right speech..."
Right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—

this, monks, is that ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient trail, traveled and followed by the seers of old. Following it, and traveling along it, I perceived aging and death, the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death.

I saw birth, becoming, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and the formative forces; I saw the arising of the formative forces, the cessation of the formative forces, and the path leading to the cessation of the formative forces.
I have seen this step by step.

Having personally realized these dharmas through my own higher knowledge, I declare them to the monks, the nuns, the laymen, the laywomen, and to others—whether they be ascetics, brahmins, wanderers, or mendicants.
Therein, even a monk who practices correctly becomes a successful one; he achieves the righteous, wholesome Dharma.
The bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who practice correctly are successful; they accomplish the righteous, wholesome Dharma.

Thus, this holy life (brahmacarya) becomes widespread, popular, and extensive, being perfectly and clearly proclaimed as far as the realms of gods and humans. Thereafter, it is dedicated at the conclusion.
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether standing on the earth or in the atmosphere,
may they always maintain loving-kindness toward all creatures and practice the Dharma by day and by night.

Through the realization of the truth with all of them, they attained the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) and manifested supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). "Well-spoken! Well-spoken! cried out everyone in a great roar. Then, that deity withdrew her miraculous manifestations, and they began to see one another; they looked at each other.
They say:
"O sir, have you come here? Have you also come?
"I have come; it is well."

Having attained their rise and acquired the necessary provisions, they said: "Venerable Sir, may we receive the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of monks within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may we lead the holy life under the Blessed One.
He, preceded by a smile, replied: "Excellent, excellent, venerable ones! Your aspiration is noble, free from despondency, and your eloquence is beautiful."
And it was said by the Blessed One: "Seeing five advantages, a wise person should indeed be intent upon the going forth.
What are the five?
Seeing that 'I shall attain my own unique goal,' a wise person should indeed be intent upon the going forth."

Considering that "I shall be honored and praised by those for whom I am a slave, a servant, one to be commanded, and one to be employed at their will," a wise person should indeed be intent upon the life of renunciation; or considering that "I shall attain the unsurpassed security of Nirvāṇa," a wise person should indeed be intent upon the life of renunciation.
Or, seeing that "while I am one who has attained the unsurpassed security of Nirvana, I shall be reborn among the gods," a wise person should indeed be intent upon the going forth;
for in many ways has the going forth been praised by the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, and the virtuous.
"Seeing that this is the path of the rightly-gone noble beings, a wise person should indeed become intent upon the life of renunciation.
"Therefore, shall you go forth in the presence of the Blessed One, or rather in mine?
They replied:
The Venerable Saṃgharakṣita said to the Blessed One:
"If that is so, come; let us go into the presence of the Blessed One. They asked, "Venerable Saṃgharakṣita, shall we go by our own supernatural power, or by yours?
Upon hearing this, the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita was distressed and reflected: "By my own power alone, they have been brought to such a state."

The multitude of virtues had been attained, yet I became like a mere raft; with a dejected and miserable countenance, he said, "Venerable ones, wait for a moment, for I have something to do. He then sat down at the foot of a certain tree, having crossed his legs in the paryaṅka posture, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "There are five advantages to great learning. What are the five?

One becomes skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense-bases, skilled in dependent origination, skilled in what is possible and impossible, and one's instruction and admonition become independent of others."

Thereupon, by striving, exerting himself, and making an effort, through the abandonment of all defilements, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, indifferent to an axe or sandalwood paste,
having split the shell of the egg of ignorance, attained the clear knowledges, superknowledges, and analytical insights, and turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor.

He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Upendra. He said to them, "Gentlemen, take hold of the corner of my robe; let us go by means of my supernatural power.
They clung to the corner of his robe, and then the Venerable Saṅgharakṣita, like a king of swans with outspread wings, departed through the air above by means of his supernatural power.

While those five hundred merchants were unloading their merchandise, they saw him and said, "Noble Saṅgharakṣita, welcome! Have you arrived? "I have arrived," he replied. "Where are you going? He said, "To the presence of the Blessed One. These five hundred sons of good family desire to go forth, to receive the full ordination and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
Thus they said, "Noble Saṅgharakṣita, we too shall go forth; please descend for a moment while we secure our goods.
The venerable Saṅgharakṣita descended, and they secured their goods.
Then, taking those thousand sons of good family with him, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
At that time, the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma.
The Blessed One saw the Venerable Saṃgharakṣita coming from afar carrying a gift, and having seen him, he addressed the monks:

"Behold, monks, the monk Saṃgharakṣita as he approaches from afar. "Yes, venerable sir; this monk Saṃgharakṣita comes bringing a gift, monks. There is no other such gift for the Tathāgata as the gift of those to be trained."

Then the venerable Saṅgharakṣita approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Saṅgharakṣita said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, these thousand sons of good family desire to go forth into homelessness within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
"May the Blessed One grant us the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a monk, out of compassion. Thus addressed,
they were spoken to by the Blessed One with the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikṣukā*).
"Come, monks, lead the holy life.
At the very moment the Blessed One finished speaking, they immediately became shaven-headed, clad in saṃghāṭī robes, with hair and beards as if seven days old had grown since their shaving,
their hands holding alms-bowls and water-pots, and they stood with the dignified deportment of monks who had been ordained for a hundred years.

And when addressed by the Tathāgata with the word "Come," they stood there with shaven heads and bodies clad in saṃghāṭī robes, their faculties immediately stilled, having been transformed by the Buddha’s mental resolve.
Then the Blessed One gave them instruction; by striving, exerting themselves, and making an effort, they [attained realization].
Through the abandonment of all afflictions, they realized arhatship and became arhats; they were free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal,

possessing minds like space or the palm of a hand, being alike toward the axe and sandalwood, having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher cognitions, and the analytical insights, turning their backs on existence, gain, greed, and honor, and becoming worthy of worship, respect, and salutation by the gods including Indra and Upendra.
Then the venerable Saṃgharakṣita questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One.
"Here, Venerable Sir, I saw beings with the form of walls, the form of pillars, the form of trees, the form of leaves, the form of flowers,
the form of fruits, the form of ropes, the form of brooms, the form of beds, the form of mortars, and the form of cooking pots—
cut in the middle and held together by a thread as they came along. What, Venerable Sir, was the karma performed by them?"
"By the ripening of what karma have they become such as this?
The Blessed One said,
"Saṃgharakṣita, those very beings performed and accumulated actions whose provisions were obtained and whose conditions have ripened."

The actions performed and accumulated by them are present like a flood and are inevitable; who else shall experience them? Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element; rather, actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Wholesome and unwholesome actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

In the past, monks, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One. He [lived] in the city of Vārāṇasī.
He dwelt at Ṛṣivadana in the Deer Park.
His disciples there were these monks, novices, and attendants.
Those beings whom you saw, Saṃgharakṣita, appearing in the form of walls, were those very monks.

They were monks who, in the past, defiled a wall belonging to the Saṃgha with phlegm; as the ripening of that karma, they have become shaped like walls. Those beings whom you saw shaped like pillars were also monks who, in the past, defiled a pillar belonging to the Saṃgha with snot; they have become shaped like pillars.
Those beings whom you saw shaped like trees, shaped like leaves, shaped like flowers, and shaped like fruits—they too were monks.
They too, having consumed the trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits belonging to the Saṅgha for their own private use,
became like those very trees, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
as for those beings whom you saw having the appearance of broomsticks made of rope.

Those monks also had used the communal ropes and brooms for their own private enjoyment; consequently, they became shaped like ropes and shaped like brooms. As for that being whom you saw who was shaped like a bowl, he was a novice monk (*śrāmaṇeraka*) who served as the distributor of drinks and was washing out a bowl (*taṭṭuka*).
Some visiting monks arrived and asked him, "Novice, will there be a drink for the Saṅgha today?

With his mind overcome by stinginess, he said, "Do you not see that I have already wiped out my bowl and drunk the drink? Having heard this, they lost all hope; with dejected and miserable faces, they departed. Because of that, he became known as Taṭṭukākāra (the Bowl-shaped One).
That being whom you saw shaped like a mortar was also a monk for whom the task of preparing a bowl had arisen.
And there, a certain novice who was an Arhat was appointed to the duty of sealing [the bowls].
He said to him, "Novice, pound a little grain in the mortar for me.
He replied, "Elder, wait a moment; I am busy, I will give it to you later.
Becoming indignant and overcome by intense agitation, he said:
"Novice, if it were permissible for me to touch this mortar, I would throw you right into the mortar and pound you, let alone that small amount of grain on the threshing floor.
That novice reflected:
"This man is possessed by a state of intense agitation; if I were to give him an answer, he would fall into even greater provocation."
He remained silent; when his outburst had subsided, he approached him and said, "Elder, do you know who I am?
He replied, "I know."
"You were ordained as a novice in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, while I am an elder monk. Even so, that which was to be done by me having gone forth has been accomplished.
What was accomplished?"
Arhatship results from the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
You are bound by all fetters; I am liberated from all fetters.
Harsh verbal action has been uttered; I confess this transgression as a transgression, so that this very karma may become attenuated and utterly exhausted.
"May it come to an end.
Because he confessed his transgression as a transgression,
he became shaped like a mortar.

Those beings whom you saw shaped like pots were formerly the attendants of the monks; while they were boiling medicinal decoctions, they were addressed harshly by the monks, and having become corrupted in mind, they broke those pots. Because of that, they have become shaped like pots.
As for the being whom you saw walking, cut in the middle and held together by a thread—
That monk, too, was one who grasped at gain; overcome by stinginess, he diverted his acquisitions:
what was intended for the rainy season retreat he diverted to the winter retreat, and what was intended for the winter retreat he diverted to the rainy season retreat.
As the ripening of that karma, he is held together only by a thread broken in the middle.
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:

"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by the venerable Saṃgharakṣita, the ripening of which karma caused him to be born into a family that is wealthy, of great fortune, and of great possessions; and by which he realized arhatship and accomplished a great service for sentient beings?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, actions were performed and accumulated by the monk Saṃgharakṣita; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flooding torrent, and they are inevitable. These actions were performed by the monk Saṃgharakṣita alone."
Who else shall experience those accumulated [actions]?

Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element; rather, actions performed ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Both auspicious and inauspicious [actions].
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

Long ago, monks, in this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, Blessed One. He [lived] in the city of Vārāṇasī.
He dwelt in dependence upon the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana. He had gone forth in this teaching as a steward (*vaiyyāpṛtyakara*).
He had five hundred co-residents, and the populace living in that mountain village was for the most part devoted to him alone; he practiced the holy life there for as long as he lived.
Yet no collection of virtues had been attained by him.
At another time, he became ill and was attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; however, he only grew weaker, and his disease did not subside.
At the time of his death, he began to make a formal vow: "By me, for as long as life lasted, the holy life was practiced under the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly awakened one."

And no collection of qualities has been attained by me; yet, by this root of merit, may I— having gone forth in the teaching of that Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, who prophesied of the young brahmin named Uttara, "Young man, when the lifespan of beings is one hundred years, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Truly and Fully Enlightened One named Śākyamuni"— through the abandonment of all afflictions, [attain my goal].
"I shall realize arhatship.
Then his co-residents approached him and asked, "Has any collection of qualities been attained by your preceptor?
He replied, "No."
They asked, "What vow was made? He replied, "This and this.
They said, "We too, having relied upon our preceptor as a spiritual friend, shall go forth in the teaching of that very Blessed One and, through the abandonment of all afflictions, realize arhatship.
Then, it was heard by the body of people living in that mountain village that this teacher was ill.
They too approached him and asked, "Has any collection of qualities been attained by the teacher?
He replied, "No.
They said:

"What vow was made by him? Tell us, what was it? They replied, "O Teacher, having relied upon you as our spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), we too shall go forth in the teaching of that very Blessed One and, through the abandonment of all afflictions (kleśa), realize arhatship.
"Monks, what do you think? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the monk serving as an attendant (vaiyyāpṛtyakara)..."
This very person was that monk Saṃgharakṣita; those five hundred co-residents who were his were indeed these five hundred sages;
and that body of people living in the mountain village was indeed these five hundred merchants.

Because he performed service there, through the ripening of that karma, he was reborn into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments; and because he made a formal aspiration at the time of death, he has realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions and has accomplished great work for those to be trained.
"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white;

and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed. Therefore, monks, having abandoned entirely black actions as well as mixed ones, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white actions. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, where did the emanated nāga youth first attain faith?"

The Blessed One said: "In this very Bhadrakalpa, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed one."

The charioteer of those to be tamed by man, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand monks—he dwelt near the city of Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣivadana.
He taught the Dharma to his disciples in this way: "Monks, these are the forest retreats, the roots of trees, and the empty dwellings."

"Meditate, monks, on remote lodgings such as mountain slopes, caves, mountain clefts, heaps of straw, open spaces, cemeteries, forests, and wilderness tracts; do not be negligent, lest you later come to regret it.
This is my instruction."
There, some monks were meditating on the terraces of Mount Sumeru;
some on the banks of the Mandākinī lotus pond; some at the great lake Anavatapta; some on the seven mountains made of gold;
and some in various villages, towns, royal cities, and capital districts.
Now, a certain recently born young nāga was being carried off by Suparṇin, the king of birds, from above the terraces of Mount Sumeru;
there he saw the monks devoted to the practice of meditation with peaceful deportment, and his mind became serene. Having conceived that faith, he formed this thought:

"These great-souled ones have been liberated from such a specific suffering. Having thus conceived a serene faith toward them, he passed away and was reborn in Vārāṇasī in a certain brahmin family devoted to the six duties. When he had been raised, nurtured, and reached adulthood, at another time he went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One. By striving with diligence...

By striving and exerting himself, through the abandonment of all defilements, he realized arhatship and became an arhat— one who is free from passion for the three realms, for whom a clod of earth and gold are equal, whose mind is like space or the palm of a hand, who regards an axe and sandalwood alike, who has shattered the eggshell of ignorance, who has attained knowledge, supernormal powers, and analytical insights, and who is turned away from existence, gain, greed, and honor.
He became worthy of worship, honor, and salutation by the gods, including Śakra and Upendra;
he then directed his attention to consider: "From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?"
He perceives that he has passed away from among the animals and been reborn among humans because he had conceived a mind of serene faith toward the great śrāvakas.

He then directs his attention to his parents, wondering, "Where are my parents? Until he sees them weeping in the abode of the nāgas, within the womb of nāga-existence; he then goes there by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
He began to ask, "Mother, Father, why are you weeping? They replied, "Noble sir, our newborn nāga boy has been carried off by Suparṇin, the king of birds; we do not know where he is.

He said, "Mother, Father, I am that very one. Having passed away and died, I have been reborn in a brahmin family devoted to the six duties, and having gone forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa..."

"Through the abandonment of all afflictions, Arhatship has been realized. Noble One, this is wonderful and marvelous! Such was that wicked man that we did not even expect him to attain a good rebirth, let alone Arhatship; yet you have attained such a multitude of virtues. Noble One, you are one who seeks almsfood."
"We too, through our merit, shall come here every day; after you have performed your meal-rites, you may depart.
He consented. Having repeatedly enjoyed divine ambrosia (*sudhā*) in the nāga-abode, he would then depart.
He had a novice (*śrāmaṇeraka*) who was his co-resident. The monks asked him, "Novice, where does this preceptor of yours go after eating?"
He said, "I do not know.
They said, "Having repeatedly enjoyed divine ambrosia in the Naga abode, he returns; why do you not go?
He said, "He possesses great supernatural power and great majesty; how can I go where he goes?"
They said,
"When he goes by means of supernatural power, you shall grasp the corner of his robe.
He replied, "Lest I fall!"
"O gentle-faced one, if even Sumeru, the king of mountains, were tied to the corner of his robe, it would not fall, let alone you.
Encouraged by them, he went to the place where that [monk] had vanished through supernatural power and stood there; then that [monk] vanished.
He [the first monk] took hold of the corner of the robe.
The two of them departed through the air above;
when they were seen by the nāgas, two seats were prepared for them and two mandalas were swept clean.
He reflected: "For whose sake has this other seat been prepared and this mandala swept clean?"
He began to look behind him and saw that novice; he said, "Son, have you also come? The preceptor has come—how excellent!
The nāgas reflected:

"This noble one possesses great supernatural power and great majesty; he will be able to digest divine ambrosia, whereas this other one will not be able to. Therefore, let ordinary food be given to him.
Thus, they gave the divine ambrosia to one, and ordinary food to the novice monk.
That novice was his bowl-bearer; he took the bowl belonging to his preceptor. A grain of rice stuck to it, and when the novice put it into his mouth, he tasted divine ambrosia.
He reflected: "Nāgas are stingy; while two were sitting together, divine ambrosia was given to one, while the novice received ordinary food."
Then, having become filled with resentment, he made a false vow:

"By this root of merit from having practiced the holy life under the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme object of offerings, may I cause this nāga to be expelled from his nāga-abode and be reborn in this very place."
Karmas that are extremely intense and fully ripened do not wait for the destruction of the body.
In this very life, water began to flow from both his hands,
and the naga’s head also began to be afflicted with pain;
he perceived this.
He said, "Noble one, this novice has conceived an unwholesome thought; please turn him back from it.
He spoke thus to that novice: "Son, these are indeed states of woe; you have conceived an unwholesome thought—turn back!
And he spoke this verse:
"This mind has become distant; I am unable to turn it back, for even as I remain right here, water flows from my hands."
Having caused that nāga to fall from that place, he was reborn right there; there, monks, faith was attained by that young nāga.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. At one time, a certain non-Buddhist ascetic went to the Jeta Grove; there he saw that a beautiful arrangement of seats had been made and excellent food and drink had been brought forth. He reflected, "Excellent indeed are the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!"

"The enjoyment of material goods is fine for us, but the enjoyment of the Dharma is what is truly excellent; therefore, I shall go forth among them. Here I have the enjoyment of material goods, but there I shall have the enjoyment of the Dharma.
Having approached a monk, he said, "Noble one, I wish to go forth."
He was ordained and received full admission by him.

The *poṣadha* of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) fell on the fourteenth day, while that of the monks (*bhikṣu*) fell on the fifteenth. On the fourteenth day he observed the *poṣadha* in the presence of the non-Buddhists, and on the fifteenth day he did so with the monks.

Later, at another time, because an intercalary day had occurred, the monks' *poṣadha* also fell on the fourteenth day. Doubt arose in him: "Should I go there, or should I observe the *poṣadha* right here?"
"I am experiencing [this]," he thought, and this realization arose in him:
"These ascetics, sons of the Śākyas, are gentle and pleasant to live with; they are my fellow practitioners of the holy life. I, however, am of bad character and difficult to live with."

"If I do not go, it is possible that they will drop my tally-stick, overturn my wooden board, turn my bowl upside down, and expel me from the midst of my fellow celibates. Thinking thus, he went into the midst of the heretics;
meanwhile, the steward stood at the end of the row of elders and questioned the monks.
He did not see him and began to ask: "Venerable ones, has any monk of such-and-such a name arrived, or has his *chanda* been brought? They replied, "No.
The Blessed One has said: [this is the case].
"The Poṣadha ceremony should be performed after surveying the four directions.
Those monks, having surveyed the four directions, performed the Poṣadha.
Then, on the following day, that monk arrived. He was asked by the monks: "Venerable one, from where have you come?"

He arrived and said, "From whom did you hear this? "From my fellow religious practitioners. "Who are your fellow religious practitioners? "The heretics. "What kind of fellowship do you have with them?
"With you, there is fellowship in material things; with them, there is fellowship in the Dharma."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks.
“Monks, this person is one who has entered the fold of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthikāvakrāntaka*). You must expel such a person from this Dharma and Vinaya.
Monks, a person who has entered the fold of the non-Buddhists is incapable of growth within this Dharma and Vinaya.

Therefore, monks, whenever anyone seeking ordination approaches, he must be asked by him: ‘Are you not one who has entered the fold of the non-Buddhists? If one grants ordination without having asked this, he commits an offense of transgression.”
It comes to be.

The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it was said by the Blessed One that a person who has entered the fold of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) is deserving of expulsion.
To what extent, venerable sir, is a person who has entered the fold of the non-Buddhists deserving of expulsion?
"Upāli, when a non-Buddhist maintains this banner and approves of that view."
And when he causes the dawn to rise therein, by this much a person who has entered among the heretics becomes one who deserves expulsion.
The setting was at Śrāvastī.
In Śrāvastī, a certain householder brought home a wife from a family of equal status; he played, took pleasure, and dallied with her.

While he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and dallying, a son was born to him. He addressed his wife: "My dear, one who pays our debts and takes over our wealth has been born to us. I shall now take merchandise and go to another country."
She said, "Noble son, do exactly so.

Taking his merchandise, he went to another country; there, through misconduct, he met with disaster. She too, by the power of her kin and the strength of her own hands, nourished, fed, and raised that son. At a later time, [he was seen] by a companion...
He was walking together with her near a certain house;
a young girl was standing at that house, and she threw a wreath of flowers over him,
whereupon he saw her.

He was addressed by his friend: "Friend, have you made an appointment with someone in this house? He replied, "Yes, I have made an appointment. His friend said, "Friend, this house is dangerous; do not enter, lest we fall into calamity through such misconduct.
Having been led about by him for the entire day, he was brought into the presence of his mother, who said: "Mother, this is your son [in] that..."

"I made an appointment with you at the house and protected you for the entire day; now protect yourself during the night, lest you enter that dangerous house and fall into calamity through imprudence.
She said, "Son, you have done well to inform us."
She prepared a bed for him in that inner room;
she brought in two earthenware pots and water and clay into that inner room, and having set up a couch at her own door, she lay down.
He said, "Mother, open the door."
"My son, for whose sake shall I urinate? He replied, "Mother, I have already placed an earthen bowl right here; urinate there."
Having stood there for a moment, he said, "Mother, open the door.
"For whose sake? [he asked].
"I shall go to the place for defecation.
She said, "Son, I have already brought a pot, earth, and water right here; defecate right here.
He stayed there for another moment and said, "Mother, open the door."
She said, "Son, do I not know where you wish to go? I cannot open the door. He said, "Mother, I shall have you killed.
She said, "Son, it would be better for me to die than to witness the murder of my own son."
"Indeed, for one who indulges in sensual desires, there is no evil deed that is not to be committed.
With a heart devoid of compassion and having abandoned the world beyond, he drew his sword from its scabbard, cut off her head at the roots, and cast it upon the ground.
Having slain her, that evil-doing being departed trembling. Then the girl said to him, "Noble son, do not fear; there is no one here but me, your servant."
He reflected, "I shall tell her; thus I will become dear to her.
He said, "My lady, for your sake I have killed my mother.
She replied:
"Is she the nurse or the biological mother? He replied, "The biological mother.
She reflected: "If one who is ignorant of virtues can even kill his own mother, what will be my own condition when he gives rise to anger toward me?"
She said, "Noble son, wait a moment; I will go up to the upper terrace and return.
He said, "Do so. Having ascended the upper terrace, she raised the cry, "Thief! Thief! Terrified by fear, he fled.
Having gone to his own home and thrown the sword at the threshold, he cried out, "This is that thief who has fled after murdering my mother!
Having paid honor to his mother, he departed;
that being, a doer of evil deeds, found no peace of mind and went to various sacred fords and groves of ascetics, where he questioned them.
"Sirs, what deed should be performed by which evil karma might go to destruction? Thereupon, one person said, "Enter the fire.
Another said, "Leap from a precipice. Another said, "Into water."

Someone said, "Tie him with a rope and he will die. Thus, they all showed him means for death, but not a single one showed him a means for liberation. At another time, he went to Jetavana, where he saw a monk engaged in recitation.
"He whose evil deed is covered over by wholesome action shines forth in this world like the moon released from a cloud.
He reflected thus.
"It is possible to block evil karma, but not to exhaust it; among these [options], I shall go forth as a monk and exhaust it.
He approached a monk and said, "Noble one, I wish to go forth. He was ordained and received full admission by that monk.
Exerting himself with extreme vigor, he began to study;

as he studied and recited, he mastered the three baskets (*tri-piṭaka*) and became a master of the Tripitaka, a preacher of the Dharma possessed of ready and eloquent inspiration. He was asked by the monks, "Venerable one, what do you aspire to through this exertion?"
He said, "I am expiating an evil deed.
[The other asked,] "What evil deed have you committed?
[He replied,] "My mother was killed."
"Is it the nurse, or is it the mother? He replied, "The mother.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, you must expel from this Dharma and Vinaya the person who has killed his mother. Monks, a person who has killed his mother is incapable of growth in this Dharma and Vinaya.
Therefore, monks, whenever anyone seeking ordination approaches, he must be asked by that [monk]: 'Are you a matricide?'"
If one causes someone to go forth without having asked [for permission], one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (sātisāra).

He reflected, "Why should I now go forth [into homelessness]? I shall go to a border region. Having gone to a border region, he converted a certain householder; being inspired with faith, that householder built a monastery for his sake.
He was inhabited by monks dwelling in various directions and regions, and through his instruction, many realized arhatship.

At a later time, he became ill; though he was attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, he only grew weaker. He said to his co-residents, "Venerable ones, prepare a steam-heated cell for my sake."
With those materials, a steam-bath house was constructed for him.
All accumulations end in exhaustion; all elevations end in a fall; all unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death.
Having passed away and died, he was reborn in the Avīci great hell.
His co-resident, an Arhat, began to reflect: "Where has my preceptor been reborn?
He began to survey the gods but did not see him; he surveyed humans, animals, and hungry ghosts, yet he did not see him there either.

When he began to survey the hells, he saw that [the teacher] had been reborn in the great Avīci hell. He reflected: "The preceptor was virtuous, learned, and maintained a following through the Dharma;
what deed did he commit by which he was reborn in the great Avīci hell? As he began to investigate, he saw that he was a matricide.
Touched by the rays from the Avīci hell, he said, "This heat of the fire in the *jentāka* (sauna) is extremely intense.
Then, the hell-warden struck him on the head with a mallet and said, "O unfortunate one, where is there a *jentāka* for you here? This is the great hell of Avīci!
Struck by the mallet, his mind became virtuous and he passed away, being reborn among the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm.
It is indeed the nature of things that when a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods has recently been reborn, three thoughts arise:

"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma? He sees: "I have passed away from the hells and have been reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings, having performed a steam-bath for the Saṅgha.
Then, this thought occurred to that son of the gods who had previously been in hell: "It would not be fitting for me to remain here with my stay [in the divine realm] already completed."
"I should go to see the Blessed One; what if I were to go to see the Blessed One even before my period of probation has expired?

Then the son of the gods who had formerly been a denizen of hell—wearing shimmering, stainless earrings, his body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, his lap filled with divine flowers such as blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, and māndārakas, and possessing a transcendent complexion—[approached].

When the night had passed, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and scattered flowers over the Blessed One, he bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down to one side. At that moment, through the power of the divine son who had formerly been a denizen of hell, the entire hall of peaked-roofed pavilions was suffused with a sublime radiance.
(Pravr-v IV 33) Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the son of the gods who had formerly been a denizen of hell,
gave such a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths; having heard it, the son of the gods who had formerly been a denizen of hell—
Seated on that very same seat, having shattered with the vajra of wisdom the mountain of the view of a self-identity— which rises with twenty peaks— he realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truth, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times:

"Venerable Sir, this which has been done for us by the Blessed One was not done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our deceased ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives; namely, that the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up, the mountains of bones have been crossed over, the gates to the lower realms have been closed, and the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened."
He has been raised up from the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, and his feet have been established among gods and humans;
and it is said:
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many defects, has been closed;

the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened, and the path to Nirvana has been found by me. And by relying upon you, I have today attained the pure, utterly stainless eye that is free from all faults.

I have attained the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones, and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering. O Sage, today your vision has borne fruit for me—your vision which is worshipped in the world by Daityas, humans, and gods; which is free from birth, old age, death, and disease; and the sight of which is so difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes.
Then, bowing down and having prostrated at both feet with his long necklace hanging low, he was filled with joy;
and having paid homage to the Conqueror of Enemies who faces the south, he departed for heaven, directed toward the world of the gods.
Then the son of the gods, formerly a denizen of hell, was like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, or like a hero.

Like one who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease, he returned to his own residence with the same splendor with which he had approached the presence of the Blessed One. Seated at the head of the meal was his fellow-resident, the Elder of the Saṅgha, an Arhat; and there was also another fellow-resident of his.
He was distributing drinking water to the Saṃgha.
When the senior monk of the Saṃgha took some water in a bronze bowl, his fingertip touched it; it was exceedingly cold.
He reflected: "We indeed drink such water as this, yet our preceptor will have to drink boiling molten copper in the great Avīci hell!"
He began to look toward the great Avīci hell, but he did not see animals or hungry ghosts;

nor did he see humans or other hells, even though he looked there. Finally, he began to look toward the gods and saw that he had been reborn among the Cāturmahārājika gods, having become a god in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having realized the truth, he remained elevated among the gods;
preceded by a smile and having attained serene confidence in the Blessed One, he uttered this inspired exclamation:
"O, the Buddha!"
"O Dharma! O Saṅgha! O how well-proclaimed is the Dharma, that even such evildoers as these, having fallen into ruin, can now attain such a multitude of virtues!
(Pravr-v IV 34)

He was seen by that fellow preceptor, who was thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, and he said to him, "Venerable one, why are you so delighted? Your preceptor has passed away and I have become the senior of the Saṅgha.
He replied, "Venerable one, it is not yet the time for you to explain this question.
You shall ask me in the midst of the Saṅgha; there will be the time for you to explain the question then."
Then, at another time, when the community of monks was seated together in assembly, the elder of the Saṅgha asked that fellow-student: "Venerable one, what did you say on that occasion?
He replied: "I said to you, 'Are you satisfied, Upādhyāya? Your preceptor has passed away and I have become the elder of the Saṅgha.'"

"We have been robbed by thieves!

Having equipped his fourfold army— the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry— and having set them in array,

Virūḍhaka surrounded them on all four sides and terrified them with the sounds of conchs and drums from the center. Some of them abandoned their plunder and fled; some were killed; but sixty were captured alive.
Taking both them and the plunder, he went into the presence of the king and said, "Your Majesty, these are the thieves, and this is the plunder."

They said:

"I shall show you that which has never been shown by anyone before.

Later on, at another time, when the monks were going on a tour of the charnel ground, he also went with them on that tour of the charnel ground.
